Kada’s built-in helper was started with the USB start command. On most phones it keeps running after you unplug the cable; on some systems unplugging stops it. If that happens, plug in and run the command again to restore phone control. Keep “USB debugging” (in Developer options) on; turning it off stops phone control. After a phone restart the helper doesn’t come back by itself: open Kada and run the command again (you can copy it in “Set up phone control”). If this phone has a working “Wireless debugging”, pairing once lets Kada reconnect by itself after restarts.

Kada uses Accessibility to read the text and buttons on screen. With this on, Kada turns on its own accessibility service in system settings for you; other accessibility services you have on aren’t affected. Turn this off and Kada turns its own service off.

After Wi-Fi drops or the phone restarts, the system turns “Wireless debugging” off. Phone control normally doesn’t need it — only when restarting (for example after a Kada update). With this on, in those moments and while on Wi-Fi, Kada turns it on and reconnects, but never turns it off for you. This uses the same “Modify system settings” permission as “Restore after restart” and works only on Wi-Fi you’ve allowed. Turn it off and Kada stops doing this.

With this on, Kada adds itself to the system’s battery optimization exceptions, so it isn’t stopped in the background to save power and phone control drops less often. It may use a bit more battery. Turn it off to go back to the system default.

“Wireless debugging” turns itself off after a restart. With this on, Kada turns it back on at startup and reconnects. This needs the “Modify system settings” permission, used only to turn on Wireless debugging, and works only on Wi-Fi you’ve trusted. Turning this off or unpairing returns the permission.
